activities.title: Sentence detectives: subject and verb
activities.outcome: Identify the subject and main verb in short everyday sentences.
activities.procedure: Display six short sentences about familiar activities. Model how to ask who or what the sentence is about, then identify the action or state. Learners underline the subject once and circle the verb. In pairs, they sort sentence cards into clear subject–verb pairs, then explain one choice.
activities.model: Example: "Mina reads." Subject: Mina. Verb: reads. In "The small dog sleeps," the complete subject is "The small dog" and the main verb is "sleeps."
activities.task: Write eight original sentences about a familiar topic. Underline each subject and circle each main verb. Include two sentences with a longer subject.
activities.success: Look for a subject and a finite verb in every sentence; check that the sentence expresses a complete idea.

activities.title: Build a sentence: word order
activities.outcome: Arrange words into grammatical statements and questions.
activities.procedure: Give learners mixed-up word groups. First ask them to identify the subject, verb, and other information. Learners arrange the groups, read the sentence aloud, and explain what changes when the order changes. Finish with a short sentence-building relay.
activities.model: Example: "every morning / walks / Omar / to school" → "Omar walks to school every morning."
activities.task: Reorder ten sets, then create five new sentences using the pattern subject + verb + object/place/time.
activities.success: Sentence begins with a suitable subject; verb is in the correct position; capital letter and full stop are included.

activities.title: Be: am, is, are
activities.outcome: Choose am, is, or are in statements, negatives, and questions.
activities.procedure: Introduce three model profiles. Learners match pronouns and nouns to am/is/are, then transform statements into negatives and questions. Conduct a mingle or simulated chat in which learners ask and answer simple personal-information questions using fictional profiles if they prefer.
activities.model: Examples: "I am ready." "She is not late." "Are they students?" Short forms: I'm, he's, we're, isn't, aren't.
activities.task: Complete a profile paragraph with the correct form of be. Write four true or fictional sentences and two questions.
activities.success: Correct subject–verb choice; appropriate negative or question order; punctuation.

activities.title: Articles: a, an, the
activities.outcome: Use a/an for a non-specific singular countable noun and the when the reference is known or specific.
activities.procedure: Show familiar objects and name them. Model the sound-based a/an choice and contrast first mention with a known item. Learners describe a picture, first introducing objects and then referring to them again with the. Discuss examples where no article is used only when suitable for the level.
activities.model: Example: "I saw a bird. The bird was on a wall." Use "an" before a vowel sound: an apple, an hour.
activities.task: Write a 90-word description of a room or picture. Introduce at least six objects and refer back to at least three using the.
activities.success: Article choice is generally appropriate; learner understands that a/an is not chosen only by spelling.

activities.title: Plural nouns and spelling patterns
activities.outcome: Form regular plurals and recognise common irregular forms.
activities.procedure: Sort nouns into regular -s, -es, consonant + y, and irregular groups. Model the spelling change and pronunciation. Learners label pictures, then use plural nouns in short descriptions. Include a short pronunciation check for /s/, /z/, and /ɪz/ endings.
activities.model: Examples: book/books; box/boxes; city/cities; child/children; person/people; mouse/mice.
activities.task: Write ten singular-to-plural changes and a short paragraph describing a group of objects or people.
activities.success: Correct spelling pattern; agreement between plural subject and verb; intelligible ending pronunciation.

activities.title: Present simple: routines and facts
activities.outcome: Describe routines, habits, and general facts using correct verb forms.
activities.procedure: Use a visual daily timeline to elicit verbs. Model affirmative forms, third-person -s, negatives with do/does, and questions. Learners interview a partner or use a fictional character schedule, then report two findings.
activities.model: Examples: "I study at night." "Lina studies at night." "Does he work on Fridays?" "She doesn't drive."
activities.task: Write a 100-word routine paragraph and create five questions for a classmate or fictional character.
activities.success: Third-person agreement; do/does support; adverb placement; routine meaning.

activities.title: Adverbs of frequency
activities.outcome: Place always, usually, often, sometimes, and never appropriately.
activities.procedure: Create a frequency line from never to always. Learners place activity cards on the line and form sentences. Model placement before most main verbs and after be. Learners compare routines without judging or requiring personal disclosure.
activities.model: Examples: "I usually read after dinner." "She is often busy." "They never arrive late."
activities.task: Write eight sentences using at least five frequency expressions. Add two questions using How often...?
activities.success: Adverb position is appropriate; frequency meaning matches the chosen expression.

activities.title: Present continuous: actions now
activities.outcome: Describe actions happening now or around the present.
activities.procedure: Show an action picture or mime an activity. Elicit be + verb-ing. Contrast "I work every day" with "I am working now." Learners describe pictures, ask questions, and identify spelling changes such as make/making and run/running.
activities.model: Examples: "They are playing." "Is she reading?" "He isn't sleeping."
activities.task: Describe a busy scene in 8–10 sentences and write four present-continuous questions.
activities.success: Correct be form and -ing form; use is/are in questions and negatives.

activities.title: Present simple or present continuous
activities.outcome: Choose present simple for routines/facts and present continuous for current or temporary actions.
activities.procedure: Display a weekly routine and a live scene. Learners sort sentences by meaning, underline time clues, and explain the choice. Avoid presenting time expressions as absolute rules; focus on what the speaker means.
activities.model: Example: "Nora works in a library" (usual job). "This week, she is working at home" (temporary situation).
activities.task: Complete a contrast exercise, then write a paragraph comparing a normal day with what is happening today.
activities.success: Choice matches intended meaning; forms are accurate; time clues support but do not dictate the choice.

activities.title: There is / there are
activities.outcome: Describe what exists in a place using singular and plural forms.
activities.procedure: Present a room image. Model there is with a singular noun and there are with plural nouns. Add negative and question forms. Learners describe a hidden picture while a partner draws or selects the matching image.
activities.model: Examples: "There is a lamp beside the bed." "There aren't any chairs." "Are there two windows?"
activities.task: Write a 100-word description of a classroom, bedroom, or imaginary place with at least eight uses.
activities.success: Singular/plural agreement; suitable article or quantifier; clear location detail.

activities.title: Prepositions of place
activities.outcome: Use in, on, under, behind, next to, between, and in front of.
activities.procedure: Place an object in different positions and ask learners to describe it. Model each preposition with a clear visual. Learners follow instructions to position objects, then give instructions to a partner.
activities.model: Examples: "The keys are under the book." "The café is between the bank and the post office."
activities.task: Draw a simple room or street map and write ten accurate location sentences.
activities.success: Preposition describes the relationship correctly; sentence structure is complete.

activities.title: Countable and uncountable nouns
activities.outcome: Distinguish countable nouns from uncountable nouns and select suitable quantifiers.
activities.procedure: Sort nouns into countable and uncountable groups. Model a/an and numbers with countable nouns; some, much, and a little with uncountable nouns. Discuss container phrases such as a bottle of water and a piece of advice.
activities.model: Examples: "three apples," "some rice," "a little milk," "a few books," "a piece of information."
activities.task: Create a shopping list and write a short explanation of what is needed and how much.
activities.success: Quantifier agrees with noun type; container expressions are understandable.

activities.title: Comparatives and superlatives
activities.outcome: Compare people, places, objects, and experiences using comparative and superlative forms.
activities.procedure: Model short and long adjective patterns, spelling changes, and irregular forms. Learners compare options using a shared set of facts. Ask them to justify a choice rather than only produce isolated forms.
activities.model: Examples: "A train is faster than a bus." "This is the most comfortable option." "Good, better, best."
activities.task: Write a recommendation comparing three destinations or products. Include four comparatives and two superlatives.
activities.success: Correct adjective form; than and the used appropriately; comparison supported by information.

activities.title: Past simple: regular and irregular verbs
activities.outcome: Describe completed past events using regular and common irregular verbs.
activities.procedure: Build a timeline around a fictional weekend. Sort verbs into regular and irregular forms, then practise affirmative, negative, and question structures. Highlight that did carries the past marking in questions and negatives, so the main verb returns to base form.
activities.model: Examples: "We visited the museum." "She went home." "Did they see the show?" "I didn't buy anything."
activities.task: Write a 120-word account of a memorable or invented day. Include time expressions and at least eight past verbs.
activities.success: Past forms are accurate; did + base form is used; events are in a logical order.

activities.title: Past continuous and past simple
activities.outcome: Show an ongoing past action interrupted by a shorter event.
activities.procedure: Use a story image to establish background action. Model past continuous for the ongoing scene and past simple for the interrupting event. Learners combine sentence halves and build a short narrative with when and while.
activities.model: Example: "I was walking home when it started to rain." "While they were waiting, the lights went out."
activities.task: Write a 140-word story with a clear setting, at least three ongoing actions, and three interrupting events.
activities.success: Tense choice supports the timeline; clauses are connected clearly; punctuation is controlled.

activities.title: Present perfect: experience and result
activities.outcome: Use have/has + past participle for life experience and present relevance.
activities.procedure: Contrast a finished past time with an experience at an unspecified time. Model ever, never, already, yet, and just in natural contexts. Learners interview fictional profiles or volunteer experiences and ask follow-up questions.
activities.model: Examples: "Have you ever tried kayaking?" "I've never flown." "She has just finished her project."
activities.task: Write a short profile of an imaginary person using six present-perfect sentences and two past-simple follow-up details.
activities.success: Have/has and participle are accurate; learner distinguishes unspecified experience from a finished time reference.

activities.title: Present perfect or past simple
activities.outcome: Select present perfect or past simple according to time reference and meaning.
activities.procedure: Present pairs of sentences and ask what time information is known. Learners sort finished-time expressions and experience/result contexts. Use questions that encourage explanation rather than relying only on signal words.
activities.model: Example: "I visited Rome in 2022." versus "I've visited Rome twice."
activities.task: Complete a short interview transcript, then write a 130-word account that combines life experience with specific past events.
activities.success: Verb form matches the time reference; finished past dates use past simple; experience statements use present perfect where appropriate.

activities.title: Future forms: will, going to, present continuous
activities.outcome: Choose future forms for predictions, intentions, and arrangements.
activities.procedure: Sort examples by speaker meaning: spontaneous decision, prediction, prior intention, and fixed arrangement. Model form and common contractions. Learners respond to scenarios and explain why a form is suitable.
activities.model: Examples: "I'll answer the phone." "We're going to start a club." "I'm meeting Sam at six."
activities.task: Write a realistic weekly plan and a paragraph predicting how one chosen activity may develop.
activities.success: Form is accurate; choice reflects intended meaning; time expressions are clear.

activities.title: Modal verbs: can, could, must, have to
activities.outcome: Use common modals to express ability, requests, rules, and obligation.
activities.procedure: Group example sentences by meaning. Contrast mustn't (prohibition) with don't have to (no necessity). Practise polite requests with could. Learners create a short guide to a classroom, club, or public space.
activities.model: Examples: "You must wear a helmet." "You don't have to bring food." "Could you help me?"
activities.task: Write ten rules and recommendations for a safe community event, using at least four different modal forms.
activities.success: Modal meaning is appropriate; base verb follows modal; mustn't and don't have to are distinguished.

activities.title: Should and advice language
activities.outcome: Give advice using should, shouldn't, could, and why don't you.
activities.procedure: Present everyday fictional problems. Model direct and softer advice. Learners match advice to problems, then role-play a help desk or advice column. Encourage more than one reasonable solution.
activities.model: Examples: "You should check the timetable." "You could ask the teacher." "Why don't you take a short break?"
activities.task: Write a 100–130 word advice response to a fictional learner problem. Give three suggestions and explain one reason.
activities.success: Advice is relevant and polite; modal forms are accurate; reasons are included.

activities.title: First conditional
activities.outcome: Talk about possible future situations and their likely results.
activities.procedure: Use realistic situations such as weather, transport, and study plans. Model if + present simple, will + base verb. Learners match conditions to results, then create their own chains. Explain that the if-clause does not normally take will in this pattern.
activities.model: Example: "If it rains, we'll move the activity indoors."
activities.task: Write a short plan for an event with at least six first-conditional sentences.
activities.success: Correct clause forms and comma use; result logically follows condition.

activities.title: Second conditional
activities.outcome: Describe imaginary or unlikely situations using if + past form and would.
activities.procedure: Model hypothetical questions and responses. Discuss the meaning difference between a likely plan and an imagined situation. Practise "If I were..." as a common formal or hypothetical pattern.
activities.model: Example: "If I had more free time, I would learn the guitar."
activities.task: Write a 150-word response to an imaginative prompt. Develop at least three hypothetical ideas and explain their consequences.
activities.success: Conditional structure is controlled; would is followed by base form; ideas are developed.

activities.title: Relative clauses: who, which, that, where
activities.outcome: Add identifying information using common relative pronouns.
activities.procedure: Show pairs of short sentences and combine them. Model who for people, which for things, that in many defining clauses, and where for places. Learners guess a person, object, or place from clues.
activities.model: Example: "A mechanic is a person who repairs vehicles." "This is the café where we met."
activities.task: Write ten definitions and a 120-word description containing at least four relative clauses.
activities.success: Relative pronoun fits the noun; clause identifies or describes clearly; word order is maintained.

activities.title: Passive voice: present and past
activities.outcome: Use be + past participle when the action or result is more important than the agent.
activities.procedure: Describe how a familiar product is made or how a service is organised. Compare active and passive sentences and identify when the agent can be omitted. Learners transform selected sentences and describe a process.
activities.model: Examples: "Workers package the product." → "The product is packaged." "The bridge was built in 1998."
activities.task: Write a 150-word process description using at least six passive forms.
activities.success: Be agrees with subject and tense; past participles are correct; passive is used for a clear purpose.

activities.title: Reported speech: statements
activities.outcome: Report what someone said using an appropriate reporting verb and tense shift where needed.
activities.procedure: Read a short dialogue and model how to report the information later. Explain that tense shifts are common when the reporting verb is past, but context and continuing truth can affect choices. Practise pronoun and time-expression changes.
activities.model: Direct: "I am tired," Maya said. Reported: Maya said that she was tired.
activities.task: Write a short news-style account of a fictional interview with six reported statements.
activities.success: Reporting verb and clause structure are accurate; pronouns and references are clear; tense choices suit context.

activities.title: Question forms and indirect questions
activities.outcome: Form direct questions and polite indirect questions accurately.
activities.procedure: Review auxiliary inversion in direct questions. Then contrast "Where is the station?" with "Could you tell me where the station is?" Learners complete an information gap using polite questions.
activities.model: Examples: "Do you know what time it starts?" not "Do you know what time does it start?"
activities.task: Write a short dialogue containing five direct and four indirect questions.
activities.success: Direct question order is correct; indirect clause uses statement word order; punctuation is appropriate.

activities.title: Gerunds and infinitives
activities.outcome: Use common verb + -ing and verb + to-infinitive patterns.
activities.procedure: Sort common verbs into patterns and build example sentences. Highlight that some verbs allow both forms with a meaning change, such as stop, remember, and try. Teach a manageable set rather than an exhaustive list.
activities.model: Examples: "I enjoy reading." "She decided to leave." "He stopped smoking" versus "He stopped to smoke."
activities.task: Write a short personal or fictional learning plan using eight target verb patterns.
activities.success: Verb pattern matches the selected verb; infinitive and -ing forms are spelled correctly; meaning is clear.

activities.title: Articles and determiners: advanced review
activities.outcome: Use articles, demonstratives, possessives, and quantifiers to make reference clear.
activities.procedure: Give learners a passage with missing or incorrect determiners. Ask them to identify whether the noun is specific, new, general, countable, or uncountable. Discuss cases where zero article is appropriate.
activities.model: Example: "The information in this report is useful" but "Information is important."
activities.task: Edit a 180-word passage and write a short explanation of five determiner choices.
activities.success: Choices support clear reference; countability is considered; explanations show understanding.

activities.title: Modals of deduction
activities.outcome: Use must, might, may, could, and can't to make deductions from evidence.
activities.procedure: Present a harmless fictional mystery with several clues. Model degrees of certainty and distinguish deduction from obligation. Learners compare possible explanations and justify their choices using evidence.
activities.model: Examples: "The lights are off; they might be asleep." "That can't be the correct key."
activities.task: Write a 150-word explanation of a fictional mystery using at least five deduction forms.
activities.success: Modal strength matches evidence; reasoning is coherent; verb form after modal is correct.

activities.title: Third conditional
activities.outcome: Discuss alternative past outcomes using if + past perfect and would have + past participle.
activities.procedure: Use a fictional decision with known consequences. Model the structure and explain that it imagines a different past. Learners complete sentence halves and discuss alternative outcomes without judging real people.
activities.model: Example: "If we had checked the map, we wouldn't have taken the wrong road."
activities.task: Write a reflective paragraph about a fictional project that went wrong, including four third-conditional sentences.
activities.success: Past perfect and would have forms are accurate; imagined result is logically connected.

activities.title: Mixed conditionals
activities.outcome: Connect a past condition to a present result or a present condition to a past result.
activities.procedure: Draw two timelines and compare past causes with present consequences. Model only the most useful patterns first. Learners interpret context before selecting the structure.
activities.model: Example: "If I had accepted the offer, I would live abroad now."
activities.task: Write a 180-word scenario analysis using at least three mixed conditionals and explain the time relationship.
activities.success: Time relationship is clear; verb forms fit the intended meaning; sentences remain readable.

activities.title: Cohesion: linking words and reference
activities.outcome: Connect ideas using addition, contrast, cause, result, and reference words.
activities.procedure: Give learners a paragraph cut into sections. They order the ideas and identify clues such as pronouns, repeated key terms, and linking expressions. Discuss why a connector must express the correct relationship.
activities.model: Examples: however, therefore, in addition, although, as a result, for example, this issue.
activities.task: Rewrite a disconnected paragraph with suitable links and produce a new 150-word paragraph using at least six cohesive devices.
activities.success: Links express accurate relationships; pronoun reference is clear; overuse is avoided.

activities.title: Punctuation: commas, apostrophes, quotation marks
activities.outcome: Use punctuation to make sentence meaning clear.
activities.procedure: Model punctuation in short examples. Learners identify sentence boundaries, list commas, contractions, possessives, and direct speech punctuation. Discuss how punctuation can change meaning.
activities.model: Examples: "Let's eat, Grandma." versus "Let's eat Grandma."; "the student's book" versus "the students' books."
activities.task: Edit a 160-word passage and write a short dialogue with correctly punctuated speech.
activities.success: Sentence boundaries are clear; apostrophes show possession or omission; dialogue punctuation is consistent.

activities.title: Common error clinic: agreement and tense
activities.outcome: Identify and correct recurring agreement and tense errors in context.
activities.procedure: Display anonymised example errors. Learners first identify what the writer intended, then locate the issue, explain the pattern, and correct the sentence. Emphasise that errors are evidence for learning, not a reason for embarrassment.
activities.model: Examples: "She go to school" → "She goes to school." "Yesterday I have seen..." → "Yesterday I saw..."
activities.task: Correct twelve sentences and write six original sentences that demonstrate the corrected patterns.
activities.success: Correction preserves intended meaning; explanation identifies the relevant grammar pattern.

activities.title: Grammar in authentic instructions
activities.outcome: Understand and write clear instructions using imperatives and sequence markers.
activities.procedure: Follow a short set of instructions and identify imperative verbs. Learners put steps in order and notice sequence markers. Discuss when to use positive and negative imperatives and how to make instructions polite.
activities.model: Examples: "Turn off the device." "Do not touch the hot surface." "First..., next..., finally..."
activities.task: Write a 10-step guide for a safe, familiar process. Include a title, materials, and ordered instructions.
activities.success: Steps are complete and logically ordered; imperative forms are clear; safety information is unambiguous.

activities.title: My first profile paragraph
activities.outcome: Write a short, organised introduction using basic personal information and be.
activities.procedure: Model a short profile with a name, role, interests, and one goal. Highlight capital letters, full stops, and the verb be. Learners complete a planning frame, rehearse sentences orally, and draft a paragraph. They may use a fictional identity if they prefer not to share personal details.
activities.model: Model: "Hello. My name is Alex. I am a student. I enjoy drawing and reading. I am learning English because I want to communicate with more people."
activities.task: Write 6–8 connected sentences. Include an opening, at least three details, and a closing sentence.
activities.success: Reader can understand who the writer is; sentences are complete; capitals and full stops are used.

activities.title: Describe a picture clearly
activities.outcome: Write simple sentences describing people, objects, colours, and positions.
activities.procedure: Show a picture and model moving from general to specific information: place, people, objects, actions, and positions. Learners label key details before writing. Encourage precise nouns instead of repeating "thing."
activities.model: Model: "There are two children in the park. A red ball is under the bench. One child is holding a book."
activities.task: Write 8–10 sentences describing the picture. Include at least three place prepositions and two present-continuous verbs.
activities.success: Description follows a clear order; details match the picture; target grammar is used accurately.

activities.title: A daily routine mini-story
activities.outcome: Describe a typical day using present simple and time expressions.
activities.procedure: Build a class timeline from morning to evening. Model time expressions and frequency adverbs. Learners choose a realistic or fictional character and organise events in chronological order.
activities.model: Model: "First, Sam gets up at seven. He usually eats breakfast at home. After school, he plays basketball."
activities.task: Write 100–120 words with at least six routine verbs and four time or sequence expressions.
activities.success: Events are ordered; present simple is controlled; third-person -s is checked where needed.

activities.title: A message to a classmate
activities.outcome: Write a friendly message with a greeting, purpose, details, and closing.
activities.procedure: Read two short messages and identify greeting, reason, information, and closing. Discuss audience and clarity. Learners select a scenario such as asking about homework or inviting someone to a study session.
activities.model: Model: "Hi Noor, are you free after class? I'm going to review Unit 3 at the library. Would you like to join me? See you, Lina."
activities.task: Write a message of 50–80 words. Include a clear purpose, two details, and one question.
activities.success: Message is appropriate for a friend; purpose is clear; sentences and punctuation are readable.

activities.title: My favourite place
activities.outcome: Describe a familiar or imagined place using there is/are and prepositions.
activities.procedure: Brainstorm location, size, atmosphere, objects, and activities. Model a paragraph that moves from general description to details. Learners plan with a simple mind map before drafting.
activities.model: Model: "My favourite place is a small garden. There are tall trees near the gate. A bench is under the largest tree."
activities.task: Write 100–130 words. Include a topic sentence, at least six details, and a closing sentence explaining why the place is special.
activities.success: Paragraph has a clear focus; details are specific; there is/are and prepositions are accurate.

activities.title: A past-event postcard
activities.outcome: Write a short postcard describing a completed trip or event.
activities.procedure: Examine a sample postcard and identify the greeting, place, event, and closing. Review past simple verbs and time expressions. Learners plan three events and one reaction.
activities.model: Model: "Yesterday we visited the old harbour. We walked along the water and tried a local dish. The weather was sunny, and I took many photos."
activities.task: Write 90–120 words in postcard style. Use at least eight past-tense verbs and one sentence about a feeling or opinion.
activities.success: Past events are clear and ordered; verbs are checked; tone suits a postcard.

activities.title: A recipe or how-to guide
activities.outcome: Write ordered instructions using imperatives, sequence markers, and quantities.
activities.procedure: Read a short set of instructions and identify title, materials, and steps. Model imperative verbs and sequence markers. Discuss clarity and safety. Learners choose a familiar process that is safe to explain.
activities.model: Model: "First, wash the vegetables. Next, cut them into small pieces. Then, mix everything in a bowl. Finally, serve the salad."
activities.task: Write a 10-step guide with a title, materials or preparation list, and sequence markers.
activities.success: Steps are complete and logical; verbs are imperative; quantities and warnings are clear.

activities.title: A friendly invitation
activities.outcome: Invite someone to an event and provide essential details.
activities.procedure: Review the information a reader needs: event, date, time, place, purpose, response request. Compare a friendly invitation with a formal notice. Learners invent a club or community event.
activities.model: Model: "Would you like to join our book afternoon on Saturday at 3 p.m. in Room 4? Please let me know by Thursday."
activities.task: Write an invitation of 70–100 words and a short reply accepting or declining politely.
activities.success: All essential details are present; tone is friendly; request and response are clear.

activities.title: Compare two places
activities.outcome: Compare two places using comparatives and clear categories.
activities.procedure: Choose two places with comparable information. Model a topic sentence, comparison points, and a final preference supported by reasons. Learners organise ideas in a Venn diagram or table.
activities.model: Model: "The coastal town is quieter than the capital, but the capital has more museums. I would choose the town for a relaxing weekend."
activities.task: Write 120–150 words comparing at least three features and giving a justified preference.
activities.success: Comparison uses accurate forms; ideas are grouped; preference is supported by reasons.

activities.title: A short story from three pictures
activities.outcome: Create a coherent story using past simple, sequence, and descriptive detail.
activities.procedure: Study the pictures and identify the setting, character, problem, and outcome. Model a beginning-middle-end plan. Learners draft the story and add dialogue only if ready.
activities.model: Model opening: "On Saturday morning, a young cyclist found a small bag beside the bridge. At first, nobody was nearby."
activities.task: Write 130–160 words with a clear beginning, problem, sequence of events, and ending.
activities.success: Story is coherent; past tense is mostly consistent; events connect logically.

activities.title: An email asking for information
activities.outcome: Write a polite email requesting information and asking clear questions.
activities.procedure: Show a short email and label subject, greeting, purpose, questions, and closing. Discuss polite question forms and paragraphing. Learners choose a course, event, or service enquiry.
activities.model: Model: "Dear Course Team, I am interested in your evening English classes. Could you tell me when the next course begins and whether online lessons are available?"
activities.task: Write 120–150 words. Ask at least three relevant questions and include a polite closing.
activities.success: Purpose is stated early; questions are clear and polite; email structure is appropriate.

activities.title: A balanced opinion paragraph
activities.outcome: State an opinion and support it with reasons and examples.
activities.procedure: Model a topic sentence, two supporting reasons, an example, and a concluding sentence. Discuss the difference between a reason and a repeated opinion. Learners choose a low-stakes topic.
activities.model: Model: "School clubs are valuable because they help learners practise teamwork. For example, a drama club requires members to plan and cooperate."
activities.task: Write 150–180 words with a clear opinion, two developed reasons, one example, and a conclusion.
activities.success: Position is clear; reasons are developed; linking words support the flow; examples are relevant.

activities.title: A formal request email
activities.outcome: Write a structured, polite request with a clear explanation and appropriate register.
activities.procedure: Compare informal and formal messages. Identify greeting, reason, request, supporting detail, and closing. Model indirect questions and modal verbs. Learners write to an organisation or school office in a fictional scenario.
activities.model: Model: "I am writing to ask whether it would be possible to change my appointment. I would be grateful if you could let me know which alternative dates are available."
activities.task: Write 150–180 words. Make one clear request, explain the reason briefly, and ask for a response.
activities.success: Register is consistent; request is specific; paragraphs and punctuation are clear.

activities.title: A narrative with a turning point
activities.outcome: Develop a story with setting, character motivation, conflict, and resolution.
activities.procedure: Read a short model story and identify how the writer builds expectation. Plan setting, character, goal, obstacle, turning point, and resolution. Encourage concrete detail rather than a long list of adjectives.
activities.model: Model turning point: "Just as the final bus pulled away, Leila noticed the envelope still on the seat beside her."
activities.task: Write 180–220 words. Include a turning point, varied past tenses where appropriate, and a satisfying ending.
activities.success: Story structure is clear; events are connected; detail supports mood and character; tense control is maintained.

activities.title: A problem–solution paragraph
activities.outcome: Explain a problem, its effects, and realistic solutions.
activities.procedure: Choose a manageable issue such as litter, noisy study spaces, or late transport. Model a structure: identify issue, explain effect, suggest solution, justify feasibility. Learners distinguish evidence from opinion.
activities.model: Model: "One problem is that the study room becomes noisy after lunch. This makes concentration difficult. A simple solution would be to create quiet and discussion zones."
activities.task: Write 160–190 words with one problem, two effects, and two practical solutions.
activities.success: Problem is specific; effects are explained; solutions respond directly; connectors are accurate.

activities.title: A review of a book, film, or game
activities.outcome: Summarise a work and evaluate it for a target audience.
activities.procedure: Read a short review and identify title, brief context, strengths, weaknesses, recommendation, and audience. Warn against retelling the entire plot. Learners may review a familiar work suitable for the class.
activities.model: Model: "The story is easy to follow, and the main character is memorable. However, the middle section feels slow. I would recommend it to readers who enjoy mysteries."
activities.task: Write 170–200 words. Include a short overview, two strengths, one limitation, and a justified recommendation.
activities.success: Summary is concise; evaluation is supported; audience is identified; tone suits a review.

activities.title: A short report with headings
activities.outcome: Present findings and recommendations in a clear report format.
activities.procedure: Collect or provide simple survey results. Model a title, purpose, findings, and recommendations. Teach neutral reporting language and the use of headings. Learners must not invent results; use only the provided data.
activities.model: Model: "Most respondents preferred afternoon sessions. A smaller group selected weekend classes. The results suggest that a flexible timetable may be useful."
activities.task: Write a 180–220 word report with headings and at least two recommendations based on the data.
activities.success: Report structure is clear; data is represented accurately; recommendations follow from findings.

activities.title: A persuasive letter
activities.outcome: Make a respectful case for a change using reasons and evidence.
activities.procedure: Analyse a sample letter and identify audience, request, reasons, evidence, and respectful closing. Learners choose a realistic change such as improving a shared space or adding a club.
activities.model: Model: "I am writing to suggest that the library remain open for one additional hour twice a week. This would give learners more time to study after lessons."
activities.task: Write 200–230 words. State the request, give three reasons, include one example, and propose a practical next step.
activities.success: Argument is focused; reasons are relevant; tone is respectful; paragraphs are organised.

activities.title: A compare-and-contrast essay
activities.outcome: Compare two options using a clear structure and balanced analysis.
activities.procedure: Model block organisation and point-by-point organisation. Discuss when each structure helps the reader. Learners select two options such as online and in-person learning and create a comparison matrix before drafting.
activities.model: Model thesis: "Both formats can support progress, but they differ in flexibility, interaction, and access to resources."
activities.task: Write 250–300 words with an introduction, organised comparison, conclusion, and a reasoned overall judgement.
activities.success: Thesis is clear; comparison is balanced; paragraphs have controlling ideas; conclusion follows from analysis.

activities.title: An argument essay with counterargument
activities.outcome: Develop a position, support it, address an opposing view, and conclude logically.
activities.procedure: Model claim, reason, example, counterargument, response, and conclusion. Teach learners to represent an opposing view fairly. Use supplied evidence cards or clearly labelled classroom observations.
activities.model: Model: "Some people argue that homework creates unnecessary pressure. This concern is reasonable when tasks are excessive; however, short, purposeful practice can reinforce learning."
activities.task: Write 280–330 words with a clear thesis, two developed arguments, one counterargument, and a conclusion.
activities.success: Argument is coherent; counterargument is fair; evidence is relevant; cohesion and register are controlled.

activities.title: Summarise a short source
activities.outcome: Identify main ideas and restate them concisely in original wording.
activities.procedure: Read the source twice: first for overall meaning, second to mark key points. Model how to remove examples and repetition while preserving the author's meaning. Teach learners not to insert their own opinion into a neutral summary.
activities.model: Model process: identify the central point, select two supporting ideas, combine related information, and check that the wording is genuinely the learner's own.
activities.task: Write a 100–140 word summary of the supplied text. Add the source title if requested by the teacher.
activities.success: Main ideas are accurate; unnecessary details are removed; wording is original; no unsupported claim is added.

activities.title: Paraphrase without changing meaning
activities.outcome: Restate information using different structure and vocabulary while preserving meaning.
activities.procedure: Model changing sentence structure, word class, and phrasing without replacing every word with a synonym. Discuss which technical terms should remain. Learners compare an acceptable paraphrase with a patchwriting example.
activities.model: Original: "Regular practice helps learners remember new vocabulary." Possible paraphrase: "Learners are more likely to retain new words when they practise consistently."
activities.task: Paraphrase five short statements and combine two into a concise paragraph. Keep a record of the source where required.
activities.success: Meaning is preserved; structure is meaningfully changed; key terms remain accurate; source acknowledgement follows task rules.

activities.title: A professional biography
activities.outcome: Write a concise third-person biography with accurate achievements and goals.
activities.procedure: Review sample biographies and identify name, role, experience, strengths, and current goal. Emphasise factual accuracy and avoiding invented qualifications. Learners can use a fictional profile if they prefer.
activities.model: Model: "Rania is an English learner who enjoys collaborative projects. She has volunteered at community events and is currently developing her presentation skills."
activities.task: Write 130–170 words in third person using only supplied or confirmed facts.
activities.success: Information is accurate; third-person forms are consistent; profile is concise and organised.

activities.title: A CV achievement bullet
activities.outcome: Describe experience or a project using concise action-focused language.
activities.procedure: Show weak and strong CV bullets. Model action verb + task + result where evidence exists. Explain that learners must not invent results or claim skills they do not have.
activities.model: Model: "Organised weekly study notes for a four-person project team" is clearer than "Responsible for many things."
activities.task: Write six CV bullets based on real or fictional supplied experience. Add a short skills section with evidence.
activities.success: Bullets are concise, specific, truthful, and begin with clear action verbs where suitable.

activities.title: A job application email
activities.outcome: Write a professional email introducing an application and identifying attached documents.
activities.procedure: Read a sample vacancy and identify the employer's needs. Model a concise subject line, greeting, role reference, relevant strength, attachment note, and closing. Avoid generic claims that do not match the vacancy.
activities.model: Model: "I am applying for the customer support assistant role advertised on your careers page. My experience supporting group projects has helped me develop clear communication and problem-solving skills."
activities.task: Write 150–190 words tailored to the supplied vacancy. Mention one relevant skill with evidence and identify the attached CV.
activities.success: Email is tailored; claims are supported; register is professional; structure is concise.

activities.title: A meeting summary
activities.outcome: Record decisions, key points, and actions in a concise neutral format.
activities.procedure: Run a short mock meeting or provide notes. Model separating discussion from decisions and actions. Include action owner and due date only when provided; do not invent commitments.
activities.model: Model: "Decision: The team will test the new timetable for two weeks. Action: Sam will prepare the feedback form by Friday."
activities.task: Write a 150–200 word meeting summary with purpose, decisions, and action items.
activities.success: Summary is neutral; decisions are accurate; action items are specific and grounded in notes.

activities.title: A proposal for a learning project
activities.outcome: Present a goal, rationale, plan, resources, and evaluation method.
activities.procedure: Analyse a proposal model and label its sections. Learners choose a realistic learning project, such as a reading club or language exchange. Ask them to distinguish objectives from activities and evaluation from promotion.
activities.model: Model objective: "Increase voluntary reading by offering a weekly 20-minute shared reading session."
activities.task: Write 250–300 words with a title, purpose, rationale, plan, resources, timeline, and success measure.
activities.success: Proposal is feasible; sections are complete; success measure is observable; language is appropriately formal.

activities.title: A reflective learning journal
activities.outcome: Describe a learning experience, evaluate strategies, and set a next goal.
activities.procedure: Model reflection beyond "I liked it." Use what happened, what was challenging, what strategy helped, what evidence shows progress, and what comes next. Learners can reflect on a classroom task rather than a personal event.
activities.model: Model: "At first, I found the listening task difficult because I tried to understand every word. On the second attempt, I focused on key information and identified the main idea."
activities.task: Write 150–180 words using specific evidence and one measurable next goal.
activities.success: Reflection explains learning; evidence is included; next goal is realistic and clear.

activities.title: Edit for clarity and concision
activities.outcome: Improve a draft by removing repetition, clarifying references, and varying sentence structure.
activities.procedure: Give learners a draft with repeated words, vague pronouns, and unnecessary phrases. Model reading as a reader and asking what is unclear or redundant. Learners revise in two colours: meaning changes and language changes.
activities.model: Example: "The event was good. It was good because the activities were good." → "The event was successful because the activities encouraged everyone to participate."
activities.task: Revise the supplied draft, then apply three editing strategies to one paragraph of their own.
activities.success: Revision improves reader understanding; meaning is preserved; changes are purposeful rather than decorative.

activities.title: Write a clear set of instructions for an app
activities.outcome: Explain a simple digital process using ordered steps and user-friendly language.
activities.procedure: Choose a familiar, non-sensitive app workflow. Model audience-focused instructions with action verbs, numbered steps, and expected results. Ask learners to avoid unexplained technical jargon.
activities.model: Model: "Open the Settings menu. Select Language. Choose your preferred option. Save the change and return to the home screen."
activities.task: Write 8–12 steps and include one troubleshooting note. Test the instructions with a partner if possible.
activities.success: Steps are actionable and ordered; terms are consistent; troubleshooting note is useful.

activities.title: A newsletter item
activities.outcome: Write a short engaging announcement for a defined community audience.
activities.procedure: Review a newsletter item and identify headline, key information, audience benefit, and call to action. Learners use only the facts supplied. Discuss how to make a headline informative rather than exaggerated.
activities.model: Model: "New lunchtime reading club begins next Wednesday. Learners can bring a book or choose one from the classroom collection."
activities.task: Write 120–160 words with a headline, essential details, and a clear next step.
activities.success: Information is accurate; headline matches content; tone suits the audience; call to action is clear.

activities.title: A balanced review of a service
activities.outcome: Evaluate a service using criteria, examples, and a fair recommendation.
activities.procedure: Choose a fictional service and agree on criteria such as clarity, reliability, access, and support. Model evidence-based evaluation and avoid unsupported absolute statements.
activities.model: Model: "The booking process was straightforward, although the confirmation message could provide clearer directions."
activities.task: Write 180–220 words with an overview, two strengths, one limitation, and a practical recommendation.
activities.success: Evaluation is balanced; examples support judgements; tone is fair and precise.

activities.title: A cause-and-effect essay
activities.outcome: Explain causes and consequences using logical organisation and qualified claims.
activities.procedure: Model a cause chain and distinguish immediate from long-term effects. Learners select a topic supported by supplied information. Discuss cautious language when evidence is limited.
activities.model: Model: "One contributing factor is limited access to quiet study space. This can reduce concentration, particularly when learners share crowded rooms."
activities.task: Write 250–300 words with an introduction, two causes, two consequences, and a conclusion.
activities.success: Relationships are explained; claims are qualified; paragraphs are coherent; examples are relevant.

activities.title: A source-based response
activities.outcome: Combine information from two short sources and distinguish their perspectives.
activities.procedure: Read both sources and record each central claim, evidence, and perspective. Model grouping ideas by theme rather than writing one summary after another. Teach attribution phrases and source acknowledgement.
activities.model: Model: "Both sources identify flexibility as an advantage. However, Source A emphasises access, while Source B focuses on the need for learner self-management."
activities.task: Write 250–320 words synthesising at least two shared themes and one difference. Use the source labels required by the teacher.
activities.success: Information is represented accurately; perspectives are distinguished; synthesis is organised by theme; attribution is clear.

activities.title: A short speech with signposting
activities.outcome: Write a spoken presentation with a clear opening, signposts, examples, and closing.
activities.procedure: Listen to or read a short speech. Identify attention-getter, purpose, signposts, examples, and conclusion. Teach that spoken language should be clear and natural rather than overly complex.
activities.model: Model: "Today I'd like to explain three ways to make independent study more effective. First... Another useful strategy... Finally..."
activities.task: Write a 2–3 minute speech (approximately 250–350 words depending on pace) and mark pauses or emphasis.
activities.success: Speech has a clear structure; signposts guide listeners; examples support the message; wording sounds natural aloud.
